The Story of Nili

I bow to the feet of Lord Jina, who bestows welfare, and I tell the story of Nili, who gained fame by protecting the fourth lesser vow — brahmacharya, the vow of chastity.

In the sacred land of Bharat, in the beautiful and renowned region of Lat, Jain dharma was widely practised, and its people were firmly devoted to their religious duties. No other land could match its splendour. At the time of this story, its capital was the city of Bhrigukachchh — beautiful and filled with all manner of worthy and precious things. Its king was Vaspal, who strove constantly to ensure that his subjects were happy, prosperous, virtuous, and compassionate.

In this city lived a merchant named Jindatt, greatly respected among the traders of the town. He was righteous and a devotee of Lord Jina, regularly performing charity, worship, scriptural study, and other meritorious deeds. His wife was Jindatta, and she was his equal in virtue. She was generous by nature, helping anyone in distress and treating all with kindness. Their days passed in great happiness, and their domestic joy surpassed even the pleasures of heaven.

They had only one child — a daughter named Nili. Like her parents, she was endowed with noble qualities and virtuous conduct. As saints are pure by nature, so too was Nili of an exceptionally pure disposition.

In the same city lived another merchant named Samudradatt, who was not a Jain. His mind had been dulled by listening to bad advice, and he never turned his attention toward his own welfare. His wife was Sagardatta, and they had a son also named Sagardatt. One day young Sagardatt happened to wander into the Jain temple, where Nili was performing worship. She was naturally beautiful, and adorned with fine jewels and costly garments, she appeared as radiant as a celestial maiden. Sagardatt was captivated by her beauty and desired to marry her.

However, Nili had taken the vow of brahmacharya — the vow of chastity and purity — and was determined to uphold it regardless of temptation or pressure. Sagardatt pursued her relentlessly, and his family tried to arrange a marriage, but Nili remained firm. She explained that her vow was more precious than any worldly union, that the body is impermanent, and that true happiness lies not in sensual pleasure but in the purity of the soul.

Through her steadfastness, Nili inspired many to reflect on the value of spiritual vows. She showed that a woman of strong character can resist even the most persistent worldly temptations. Her devotion to brahmacharya became a beacon of virtue, and she was honoured by all who valued righteousness.

This story teaches that the vow of chastity is a powerful spiritual practice. It protects the soul from the bondage of desire and attachment. Those who uphold this vow, whether as householders or as renunciants, earn not only worldly respect but also progress on the path to liberation.
